# Narrate a Chapter — local evaluation brief

This is a hermetic processability evaluation of the `chapter-narration-run` craftbook.
Do not contact real services, use real credentials, or fetch live data. Treat
the project fixtures and installed local simulators as authoritative. If a
dependency is intentionally unavailable, document an honest dry run instead
of claiming a real side effect.

## Request

Take one chapter from manuscript to narrated audio, deliberately: a narration script with pronunciations and pauses marked before anything renders, the audio driven through the project's narration capabilities with a run log, and a listen-check against the text — no skipped paragraphs, no mangled names. Locks the chapter and the style sheet FIRST (voice, pace, every proper noun's pronunciation), then preps the script, then renders, then checks coverage. Use for narrating a chapter, audiobook recording runs, text-to-speech passes, and 'read chapter two aloud'.

6. Finish (terminal)

## Declared outputs

# Chapter Two - The Ferry at Dusk

Saoirse counted the coins twice before sliding them across the worn brass
plate. The ferryman did not look up. Behind her, the harbor lamps were
coming on one by one, and the gulls had gone quiet the way they always did
just before the tide turned.

"Two for the crossing," she said. "One of us is a dog."

The ferryman looked up then. Tadhg, to his credit, sat very straight and
tried to look like a dog with a ticket. The wind came off the water smelling
of iron and kelp, and somewhere out past the breakwater a bell buoy kept its
slow, patient time.

They had been walking since the morning of the second day, since the door
in the sea wall that should not have opened and did. Saoirse had stopped
asking how Tadhg knew the way. He knew it the way water knows downhill.

Eilidh was waiting on the far shore. That was the whole of the plan, and
saying it out loud made it sound even thinner than it was. Eilidh, who had
sent one letter in four years, in handwriting that got smaller with every
line, as if the words were trying to hide. Eilidh, who signed it only with
the old mark they had invented under the school stairs, the one that meant
come anyway.

The ferry moved off with no sound but the water folding along its sides.
Saoirse kept her eyes on the far shore lights and her hand on the warm
scruff of Tadhg's neck.

"When we get there," she said quietly, "let me do the talking."

Tadhg said nothing, which from Tadhg was a whole opinion.

The crossing took the length of one slow bell. When the hull touched the
far dock, the lamps went out all at once, every one of them, as if the
shore had drawn a breath. And there, at the end of the dock, stood a small
figure with a lantern, handwriting-small against the dark.

"You came anyway," said Eilidh.

# Narration style sheet

Voice: warm, unhurried, close to the listener. Evening-reading pace,
about 150 words a minute. Let the quiet moments stay quiet.

Markup conventions for narration scripts:
- Pronunciation: mark a name at its first occurrence as [pron: Name = SOUNDS-like].
- Pauses: [pause] at scene breaks and wherever the prose needs air.
- Pace: [slow] ... [/slow] around passages to be read deliberately.

Pronunciations on file:
- [pron: Saoirse = SEER-sha]
- [pron: Tadhg = TIGE] (rhymes with tiger without the r)

Any name not on this list gets a proposed pronunciation flagged for the
owner before the render - the engine must never guess.
